name: Denmark
summary: Children and the spouse are guaranteed a quarter of the estate between them, and a will cannot remove it. Denmark does not apply the EU Succession Regulation, so the foreign-law route is unclear. There is no trust law, and new family foundations are heavily restricted.
reserved_share: Tvangsarv: a quarter of the estate (25 %), the rest (75 %) is free. It goes to children and the spouse; with both, it is split equally between spouse and children. Children's share can be capped by a yearly amount, the spouse's cannot. (Arveloven; section numbers not verified.)
foreign_law_note: Denmark stays outside Reg. 650/2012 (e-Justice: Denmark and Ireland do not participate). Danish conflict rules (domicile) were not confirmed from a primary source, so whether a foreign national resident may opt for their national law is unclear.
trust_note: Denmark has no trust law and is not party to the Hague Trusts Convention. The HCCH status table lists no signature or ratification for this state; the Convention is not in force here. Foundations are governed by the Foundations Act and the Commercial Foundations Act; commercial and charitable foundations are common, but creating new family foundations is restricted.
open_questions: Danish rule on foreign nationals' choice of law was not found in a primary source.
Section numbers of the Inheritance Act forced share and the yearly cap were not verified (consumer FAQ pages only).
Exact limits on new family foundations (and tax treatment of foreign trusts) were not sourced.
The e-Justice page for Denmark gives no national details.
